Global AI Brief | US moves toward 'Super Intelligence' national strategy, Apple tightens AI agent permissions at the OS level
The US is reorganizing its AI policy command center. President Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the new AI lead and will establish a 'Super Intelligence Force.' A report on AI opportunities, risks, and the government's role is due within 120 days. There is a growing trend toward integrating AI not just as industrial policy, but as intelligence and security policy.
The proliferation of AI agents has begun to change OS design. Apple is tightening 'Full Disk Access' on Mac, requiring explicit user action when AI agents or similar tools attempt comprehensive access to files, emails, messages, and browsing history. The frontier of AI safety has shifted from model companies to the OS where AI actually operates.
In the model race, NVIDIA-backed Reflection is preparing to launch a new open-weight model from the US. The target is not the top-tier models from OpenAI or Anthropic, but the open-weight market currently dominated by Chinese players. A second front in the US-China AI race has become clear: beyond the 'strongest model,' it is about who controls the AI infrastructure that companies and governments worldwide can operate themselves.
1. US establishes 'Super Intelligence Force'—AI policy moves to the command center for intelligence and security
President Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the new AI policy lead to head a cross-governmental organization called the 'Super Intelligence Force.'
FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, DoD CTO Emil Michael, and Scott Kupor, who oversees administrative management, will also participate and report directly to the President and the Chief of Staff. A comprehensive report on AI risks, opportunities, and the role the federal government should play will be compiled within 120 days.
The name is flashy, but what matters more is who was placed at the top.
It is neither a commerce-related figure responsible for fostering AI companies, nor a pure science and technology policy expert. It is the Director of National Intelligence, who oversees US intelligence agencies.
This reflects the fact that AI has become a national security issue, linked to cyberattacks, biological and chemical threats, military use, and model theft.
This is consistent with the trends of the past few weeks. The US has signed frontier AI safety agreements with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others, and the FTC has launched investigations into AI companies. Furthermore, there are moves in the US Congress to investigate whether China is accessing the model weights or confidential code of US companies.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration remains cautious about EU-style comprehensive ex-ante regulation. They are wary that regulation will delay AI development and hand the initiative to China.
Therefore, the US direction is not simply moving toward a 'government that regulates AI.'
They will allow AI companies to continue rapid development. At the same time, the government will directly monitor areas related to accidents, cyber threats, and national security.
It is more accurate to view this as the integration of AI industrial policy and AI security policy into a single national strategy.
2. Apple changes Mac permission design—AI agents are no longer just 'apps'
Apple announced on October 2 that it would introduce additional controls to 'Full Disk Access' in macOS.
Full Disk Access is a powerful permission originally intended for software like backup tools. Once granted, it largely bypasses standard per-app privacy controls, allowing broad access not only to files but also to emails, messages, and browsing history.
Apple stated clearly that as AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the risks posed by this level of access increase significantly. Moving forward, the system will be changed to require 'very explicit action' for permission, only when the user truly desires such comprehensive access. The rollout timing and specific UI have not yet been disclosed.
The background to this is the issue surrounding Meta's AI agent, Muse.
Users pointed out that Muse was accessing the contents of private messages they did not intend to authorize. Meta claims that Muse cannot read messages unless the user themselves enables the necessary system permissions and connectors, indicating a discrepancy in understanding.
However, it is not just Muse as a single product that Apple views as a problem.
Traditional apps were tools that humans launched to perform specific tasks. AI agents are different. They run in the background for long periods, operate multiple apps, read emails, search for files, and act on behalf of humans.
In other words, this is incompatible with the traditional security design of 'granting this permission to an app once'.
In the era of AI agents, the OS will need to manage not only 'what can be accessed' but also 'for what purpose, when, and to what extent access is permitted'.
Until last week, in the AI agent safety space, we have been following the issues where OpenAI and Google went outside the sandbox. Now, Apple has begun to create boundaries from the computer side, rather than the AI company side.
The AI agent race has moved from models to OS permission management.
3. NVIDIA-backed Reflection to release open models—The US takes back the market created by Chinese players
NVIDIA-backed US AI startup Reflection is preparing to release its first full-scale open-weight model soon.
According to Axios, the goal is not to outperform top-tier US closed models like OpenAI or Anthropic from the start, but to aim for performance that can compete with powerful open-weight models from Chinese players. Reflection itself has not yet announced an official release date or specifications, and its performance has not yet been externally verified.
This is quite interesting.
The US has the world's highest-level AI companies: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Even so, the presence of Chinese players has become very significant in the market for 'downloading models and running them freely in one's own environment'.
This is because DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and others have released model weights, creating an environment where companies, research institutions, and governments around the world can deploy them in their own data centers.
This is also what Reflection is targeting.
In the 'AI Factory' concept envisioned by the company, companies and governments will combine their own data, their own computing resources, and Reflection's open models to build their own AI systems.
This is also convenient for NVIDIA.
Rather than just massive cloud AI like OpenAI and Anthropic dominating the market, the demand for NVIDIA AI chips will expand if companies and governments around the world build their own AI.
For this reason, NVIDIA invested approximately $800 million in Reflection, and the company has also secured large-scale NVIDIA computing resources through SpaceX and Nebius.
In the US-China AI race, attention is focused on who will create the smartest model. However, another important factor is which AI foundation third-party countries and companies around the world will adopt.
The US side is attempting to create a full-scale counter-axis to the open-weight strategy in which Chinese players have taken the lead.
4. SoftBank acquires DigitalBridge—'Not building AI infrastructure with our own funds alone'
SoftBank Group's acquisition of DigitalBridge was completed on September 30. The acquisition price was approximately $3.1 billion. DigitalBridge is a global digital infrastructure asset management company that invests in data centers, communication towers, fiber optics, and edge infrastructure, and it will continue to operate independently under CEO Marc Ganzi after the acquisition.
The acquisition itself was announced last December; what is new is that it has been finalized and its role has become clearer.
SoftBank is simultaneously advancing massive investments in OpenAI, Arm, and AI data centers. The problem is that the scale of AI infrastructure has become too large to be covered solely by SoftBank's own balance sheet.
That is where DigitalBridge becomes significant.
The company is not just a data center firm. It is an asset management company that collects funds from institutional investors and invests them in infrastructure such as data centers, telecommunications, and power. At the time of the acquisition announcement, it was managing approximately $108 billion in digital infrastructure assets.
In other words, SoftBank has acquired not only the ability to own AI infrastructure itself but also a mechanism to attract external investor capital into AI infrastructure.
This is also common to the moves made by Amazon and Anthropic last week.
Amazon is considering a plan to move approximately $8 billion worth of AI chips to an SPV and have investors hold them. At Anthropic, Broadcom is providing up to $42 billion in financing to support a massive TPU usage contract.
When AI infrastructure investment swells to trillions or tens of trillions of yen, the capital of technology companies alone is not enough.
A financial system is needed to channel long-term capital from around the world—such as pensions, insurance, infrastructure funds, and bond investors—into AI.
SoftBank's acquisition of DigitalBridge shows that AI companies have begun to need not only 'companies that build computing power' but also 'companies that gather global funds for computing power'.
5. AI investment could exceed $30 trillion by 2050—'Can it be recovered?' is the next issue
And over the weekend, a fairly important question regarding AI infrastructure investment itself also emerged.
According to multiple estimates compiled by Reuters, global data center-related investment could exceed $30 trillion by 2050. AI companies and hyperscalers must generate enough productivity improvements and new revenue to justify such capital expenditures.
This is slightly different from the simple debate of 'is it an AI bubble?'
Railroads, power grids, and the internet were all real technologies that changed society. However, if infrastructure investment gets too far ahead, investors can lose money even if the technology is real.
The same problem has emerged with AI.
Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and others are building data centers on a scale comparable to power plants. Anthropic is reserving over $100 billion in future computing power. OpenAI and SoftBank also have even larger plans.
The question is what to sell based on that computing power.
It is difficult to recoup tens of trillions of dollars in infrastructure costs through monthly chat AI fees alone. Therefore, the market needs to expand to the point where AI agents replace corporate work, AI for Science creates new drugs and materials, and Physical AI automates manufacturing, logistics, and transportation.
In other words, AI infrastructure investment is predicated on the assumption that AI agents and Physical AI will become truly massive markets.
This is one of the reasons why AI companies have been rushing to release agents into the real world over the past few months.
If AI ends up being nothing more than 'useful software,' current infrastructure investments are too large.
Only if AI can capture massive existing markets—such as corporate labor, scientific research, manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare—will the math finally add up.
In the AI competition of autumn 2026, just as important as 'what AI can do' is the question of whether AI can create enough economic value to recoup this massive investment. that has begun to emerge as a critical question.
Connecting the five items from the start of the week reveals that the AI industry has entered its next phase.

pages.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 - Why It's Still the Best
pages.text:
From its very first iteration, the Apple Watch Ultra quickly became my favourite smartwatch.
The base model Apple Watch had already impressed me with its seamless integration with the wider Apple ecosystem.
Although it's a little frustrating to have a watch that will only pair with an iPhone, at least that means everything dovetails together flawlessly. There are very few smartwatches out there that let you read and reply to emails, texts and other DMs, including opening pictures and other attachments on the watch screen itself. Likewise, other apps like contactless payments and customer loyalty cards work so reliably that I find it quite frustrating when I'm reviewing other devices that don't work so well.
I was excited by the add-on abilities the Watch Ultra brought to the table; a more durable design, better GPS tracking and vastly superior battery life to name a few.
And while both the Ultra 2 and 3 further refined the original design, I've found it hard to recommend an upgrade for those who were already enjoying the benefits of the first model. It's rare to get a product so very-nearly perfect, first time out - and then it's hard to improve on that.
Until now.
You could be forgiven if you're thinking this is just the same Watch Ultra as last time and the time before that. From the front, it's true; very little has changed.
In fact, the Watch Ultra 4 doesn't even come in a new range of colours. The choice is still Black or Natural titanium. Yes, there are several new bands to choose from and the Translucent range of Ocean Bands are particularly unique. I was sent a Burgundy Trail Loop to pair with my review Watch Ultra 4. The Trail Loop is a very comfortable, lightweight nylon band that stretches a bit, so you can keep it nice and stuck for more accurate health and fitness tracking.
Overall, this year's colour range on the new bands tends towards more muted, natural tones - the browns, oranges and greys reminiscent of a late 1970s Anchorman-style news show set. As usual, if that's not your vibe, there are plenty of third-party options out there.
The Always-On squircle-shaped Retina display is still one of the biggest around, protected by incredibly tough sapphire crystal. It can achieve peak brightness of 3,000 nits, so it stays super clear, even on bright white snow days, or during midsummer surf sessions. It can also dim right down to just 1 nit, so you can avoid lighting up the whole bedroom when checking the time in the middle of the night.
And unlike the "ordinary" Apple Watch, the Ultra 4 still has a large, orange Action button on the left side you can customise to perform a shortcut of your choice - perhaps launch your favourite workout or open the Translate app.
Fantastic. This is all great. But none of it is new.
However, turn the Watch Ultra 4 over and you'll begin to see just how much has really changed with this device.
Just physically, you'll see there are now 8 LED sensors where there were just four previously, while the number of electrodes has skyrocketed from two to 32. There are also four photodiodes in a ring - making this the most accurate watch Apple has ever produced - and perhaps the most accurate health and fitness tracker on the market.
The beefier, yet more efficient S11 chip collates all the information this impressive raft of new sensors detects into metrics that are more detailed and useful than ever.
Because heart rate is being monitored fifty times more frequently, Heart Rate Variation (HRV) is picked up right away - not just at night while you're asleep. This can be a great indicator of either improving fitness or an advanced warning of deteriorating health.
Even the pedometer - that most fundamental of any tracker's abilities - is more accurate, and can now log your steps correctly if you're walking while keeping your hands in one position - for example, holding a drink bottle or perhaps pushing a pram or stroller.
A more efficient chip means better battery life - and that's an upgrade on something the Watch Ultra was already leading the way on. Yes, there are plenty of trackers (and even a few genuine smartwatches) that will last for days or even weeks between charges - but not with this level of functionality. Apple suggests you'll get up to 50 hours of "normal" use on a full charge and that certainly matches up with my testing.
What's more, the Watch Ultra 4 charges faster than before too - using the charger included in the box. Just 15 minutes of charging can result in an 18 hour boost. That means I hardly take it off. A quick top-up while I read a few chapters of my book before bed is really all it takes to keep my Ultra 4 running all through the night and the following day.
That's more important than ever, because not only does Watch OS now feature a far more detailed Vitals app, bringing all your metrics together in one easy-to-follow interface, including sleep data, workouts and stats like HRV, skin temp and blood oxygen levels - Apple takes it all one step further with a daily Readiness score. A quick glance reveals your mark from 1-10 and a brief explanation on why you scored what you did.
I'm sitting on 8 today, thanks to plenty of activity over the weekend and a decent night's kip last night.
And the best is yet to come. Quite literally.
Apple has been doing a lot of work behind the scenes to evolve Siri into a digital assistant with genuine artificial intelligence. The idea is your questions and requests are not only responded to as quickly as possible, but in a more natural, conversational way.
Again, on the Watch Ultra 4, the S11 chip's neural processing abilities come into play here and already I've been impressed with the notable jump in reaction time when it comes to using my watch to control IoT devices like my garage door and bedside lamp.
But in the coming months, even smarter features are coming to Apple Watch. Live Rewind will transcribe the last 15 seconds of conversation as picked up by the Ultra 4's microphone array, in case you missed the bartender explaining tonight's cocktail special, or your vet giving you instructions on which pill to give your dog when.
Actually, for something as important as that, another pending feature, Siri Recap, is probably more appropriate, listening and summarising all the important events of your day, from lectures or meetings to that list of jobs that need doing around the house.
Of course, there's also the new Siri Modular watch-face to give you instant access to some of these new apps and functions.
Ultimately, although the Watch Ultra 4 doesn't look a whole lot different, I'd argue this is the biggest upgrade since the original launched in 2022. Between the new sensors, more accurate tracking, extended battery life and the beefed-up chip, if you do decide to trade up, you'll definitely notice the improvements.

Adam Blevins began working in the entertainment industry in 2022 as a Staff Writer for Agents of Fandom, where he progressed to Senior Editor and interviewed talent from Marvel Studios, House of the Dragon, and Planet of the Apes. He joined Collider as a News Author in April 2024, was promoted to a Senior position in December 2024, and has written over 3,000 articles for the site, including exclusives relating to Avengers: Doomsday, The Penguin, Star Wars: Skeleton Crew, and more. He primarily writes about the latest box office numbers and the hottest movies and TV shows on streaming, while also covering superhero and sci-fi news. He has completed a set visit for The Chosen and even has several months of experience writing Gaming Features at ScreenRant. You can find him on X, LinkedIn, and Muckrack.
In the last few years, Apple TV has developed a strong reputation for having some of the best original TV shows any platform has to offer. Where the streamer has especially excelled is in the sci-fi genre, where it just recently introduced its most popular show of all time in Pluribus. Season 1 of Pluribus, which hails from creator Vince Gilligan (Breaking Bad), shattered records on its way to becoming the most-watched Apple TV series ever. The streamer has already confirmed that another season is on the way, though it’s still unclear at this time when it will be released. Apple TV also found success this summer with the premiere of Silo Season 3, the hit sci-fi series starring Rebecca Ferguson. The fourth and final season of the show is expected to begin streaming next summer.
The show that Pluribus had to beat to take the sci-fi streaming crown was Severance, which stars Adam Scott and Britt Lower in leading roles. Comedy icon Ben Stiller also works as the lead director on the series and one of the head producers who is heavily involved in creative decisions for plot and characters. After the first season of Severance dropped all the way back in 2023, Apple TV finally brought the show back for its second season last year, even renewing it for Season 3 on the day of the Season 2 finale. Now 18 months removed from the end of Severance Season 2, there’s still no word yet on when the show will return. However, it’s staging yet another streaming resurgence on Apple TV, where it has once again become one of the most-watched shows in the world.
Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars
Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.
You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.
APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.
In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.
AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.
What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.
AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.
How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.
ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.
Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.
AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.
Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.
AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.
Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.
AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.
What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.
AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.
Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.
You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.
You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.
You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.
You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.
The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.
The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.
You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.
You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.
You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.
In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.
You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.
You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.
In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.
You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.
In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.
Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.
Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.
You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.
Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.
In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.
The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.
You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.
You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.
You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.
In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

Apple event 2026 recap: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and more
Apple unveils its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo
Apple saved the best for last at its biggest launch event of the year on Wednesday, unveiling the foldable iPhone Duo.
CEO John Ternus made his big debut, unveiling the iPhone 18 Pro, Airpods 5 and Apple Watch Series 12 before getting to the Duo, the company's first foldable iPhone.
Apple showcased a new set of colors for the iPhone 18, which comes in glacier and burgundy, following in the success of last year's electric Cosmic Orange colorway.
First impressions of the iPhone Duo — Apple's biggest iPhone redesign ever
Customers are looking at a premium price for Apple's latest devices, with the iPhone 18 Pro and Max getting a $100 hike over last year's models. The foldable Duo starts at $1,999.
The company raised prices on Macs and iPads over the summer as memory and storage costs have soared.
What you need to know:
Apple's first foldable iPhone starts at $1,999
Apple Watch is listening to your conversations
You will be paying $100 more for iPhone 18 Pro
AI image check with Apple Reference Image
The first product launch is the iPhone 18 Pro and Max in new colors
Ternus says the iPhone is the best device for AI
Apple Event product unveil on Sept. 9th, 2026.
Apple Inc.
Thanks for following the action with us!
Big shoutout to all the readers who joined us today. Thanks for hanging out and following along with the latest announcements from Apple.
We'll have more coverage of Apple's announcements on CNBC TV with analyst and trader reactions. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream.
C2 modem in iPhone Duo further reduces Apple's reliance on Qualcomm
A man records images of the new foldable iPhone Duo on display during Apple's event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino, California, U.S. Sept. 9, 2026.
Apple just unveiled the C2 modem, which will power connectivity inside the folding iPhone Duo.
This is the second-generation modem Apple has made in-house, in a move that further reduces reliance on cellular modem leader Qualcomm.
"With our fully integrated approach, it's optimized to improve everyday user experiences, including using AI algorithms to improve cellular reliability, like reconnecting faster in low coverage areas," Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, said in the keynote video.
C2 is 50% faster than Apple's previous modem, and adds 5Gmm support in the U.S. while running at 15% lower energy, according to Srouji.
Chip analyst Ben Bajarin told CNBC in an interview that Apple will likely eliminate Qualcomm chips altogether in next year's iPhone 19 line.
Apple stock down during 'Surprise and Shine' event
Apple's new introductions, including Siri AI and the iPhone Duo, failed to impress markets. For almost the entire duration of the near-80-minute presentation, the company's stock price was down.
Opening at $315.49 today, it popped briefly to $318 and then quickly dropped.
Year-to-date, the stock is up about 15%.
Apple Inc.
Apple said its iPhone duo will cost $1,999, in line with competitors and lower than much of what Wall Street was expecting.
It will hit store shelves on Oct. 23.
Apple Inc.
Apple's marketing chief Joswiak said that the outer display of the Duo was 90% the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro, and the inner display is 7.6-inches.
The phone will use a fingerprint sensor built into the side button for unlocking. Its case is made out of titanium.
Craig Federighi, senior VP of Software Engineering, said that Apple had redesigned much of its iOS software to take advantage of the two screens, moving buttons and other controls. Users can multitask with two apps at the same time and can use Apple's stylus called Pencil.
"We looked at every aspect of iOS to see how we could make it even more useful on iPhone Duo," Federighi said.
Here's Apple's foldable phone: iPhone Duo
Apple Inc.
It's official, Apple is making a foldable phone.
"For a device that plays such a central role in your life, a larger display would open up entirely new possibilities," Ternus said. "We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design."
He said that other foldables feel like "two phones awkwardly stuck together."
Apple's phone is about the size of a passport and has an internal and external screen.
Apple Inc.
Apple Inc.
Apple Watch did not get a price increase. Series 12 will cost $399 and up, and the Ultra 4 starts at $799. Apple also announced a new version of the Apple Watch with a ceramic case.
Apple Watch can record and summarize your conversations
Apple Inc.
Apple is making its Apple Watch Series 12 into an AI device with a new feature called Audio Intelligence.
The feature will use the Apple Watch's microphone to record conversations and allow the user to review things that were just said.
"We've all been in situations where you've missed a key detail of what someone just said and wished you could go back. Now you can use live rewind, which lets you go back in time for 15 seconds," said an Apple representative in the video.
It will also be able to summarize your important conversations with a feature called Siri Recap.
"It uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference. Conversations will have an Apple Intelligence-generated title, summary, and key points," Apple said.
Apple said the feature would be private and would not store audio recordings or share them with Apple.
The features will be available in beta later this year.
Apple adds lots of new health features to Apple Watch
Apple Inc.
Apple redesigned a lot of the health features in its Health iPhone app with AI-powered coaching.
"Each morning, Apple Watch analyzes your recent activity, vitals, and sleep to give you one score with a clear call on your body's capacity to take on the day," Apple's Sumbal Desai said.
It's expected to launch later this year.
More details on the A20 Pro, Apple’s first 2nm iPhone chip for better heat controls and on-device AI
A20 Pro is Apple’s first 2nm iPhone chip enabling on-device AI
Apple unveiled its new A20 Pro system on a chip for iPhone 18 Pro. It's the first high-volume smartphone processor to be made on Taiwan Semiconductor 2 nanometer, the leading chip manufacturer's most advanced node. While 2nm chips can only be made in Taiwan, Apple has committed to make some iPhone chips on TSMC's new fabs in Arizona, too.
The A20 Pro is meant to optimize AI on-device, as Apple races to catch up in the AI race by relying on the security and privacy of avoiding the cloud. The A20 Pro is a system on a chip, or SoC, with central and graphics processors and memory integrated together, and it has a dedicated AI accelerator Apple calls a Neural Engine, to optimize that AI on device.
The A20 Pro has a six-core CPU that Apple said runs up to 20% faster, with neural accelerators to power low-latency on-device AI workloads. Its new GPU has seven cores for up to a 40% increase in performance.
Memory took a big leap too, with a 50% increase in bandwidth and what Apple said is the "widest memory interface we've ever shipped in an iPhone." Apple got there by redesigning the chip to place the core logic silicon side-by-side with the memory chips.
Memory optimization is key in the midst of a global memory shortage, as all the biggest players race to secure memory supply from giants SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron. It's also why Apple raised prices on MacBooks and iPads in June.
Apple Inc.
Apple announced new AirPods models called AirPods 5.
These new devices have a longer battery life and have active noise cancellation, which previously wasn't available on the least expensive AirPods. They cost $129, and there's a version with wireless charging that retails for $149.
Apple Inc.
iOS 27 will include a new feature that allows customers to use a single phone number across multiple devices, dubbed "iPhone Handoff."
According to Kaiann Drance, vice president of iPhone Marketing, "the number is instantly active on whichever iPhone you pick up."
She added that the feature will launch with T-Mobile and Deutsche Telekom, with Verizon and EE adding support by the end of the year. More carriers will follow.
iPhone 18 Pro gets a $100 price increase
Apple Inc.

pages.title: Everything Apple Announced: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods 5  | WIRED
pages.text:
It’s a brand-new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: It announced its first-ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport-sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new-tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhone 18s) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
As expected, Apple is not releasing a base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They feature Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new, redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all-new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video-capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.
The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.
Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

A steady monthlong climb has put a bigger round number on the radar for Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL | AAPL Price Prediction) shareholders. Apple stock is up 10% over the past month to $340 in afternoon trading, and the natural follow-up is what it would take to reach $350. Answering that requires looking past the chart to what Wall Street’s consensus expects, how Apple compares with its peers, and what Apple is actually selling. For the full-sector context, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), a fund that tracks the NASDAQ 100, is up 5% over the past month to $744.21; thus, in percentage gains, the QQQ ETF trails Apple over that stretch. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stock is up 32% over the past month to $751.41, running far ahead of Apple over the same window. Against that pace, the gain in Apple stock looks modest, even though it exceeded the fund’s advance. On the other side of the equation, Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock is down 0.7% over the past month to $344.17, which leaves Apple sitting in the middle of its own group. Complicating things further, the analyst consensus target on Apple stock is $328.22, which sits below the current share price. Getting Apple stock to the headline number likely requires analysts to raise that consensus first, since the level in question sits above a price the average target hasn’t yet reached. Apple Pitches the Mac for Local Artificial Intelligence Apple is positioning its newest Mac desktops to run demanding artificial intelligence models locally, saving buyers a cloud provider’s fee for each use. According to Apple, the new machines carry substantially more unified memory and bandwidth than the desktops they replace. Those upgrades matter. Large artificial intelligence models lean heavily on fast memory, and more of it lets a single computer handle work that might otherwise go to a data center. The pitch comes down to cost. For steady workloads, cloud usage bills keep accumulating, and Apple argues capable hardware makes more financial sense over time. Apple bulls argue that local artificial intelligence gives buyers a concrete reason to pay up for more powerful Macs. That would turn a cost argument aimed at cloud providers into hardware demand Apple can actually book as revenue. Steady Mac orders of that kind would give analysts a tangible reason to revise their targets on Apple stock. However, the consensus target on Apple stock sits beneath the current share price, so the headline level asks the market to pay more than the average analyst thinks Apple is worth. A single strong product showcase can generate excitement, yet Apple needs sustained buying before the analyst math changes. What it would take is consistent Mac sales. They need to show up in Apple’s results quarter after quarter, strong enough to push analysts into lifting the consensus above the current share price. Local artificial intelligence gives Apple a credible sales pitch; the next step is proving buyers act on it at scale. Investors drawn to the local artificial intelligence story should size positions reasonably, since Apple stock already trades above the average analyst target. Balancing exposure against other mega-cap holdings can limit damage if Mac demand proves less durable than hoped. Shareholders may want to watch for signs that Mac demand tied to local artificial intelligence repeats in Apple’s upcoming quarterly reports. Those reports will reveal if analysts start lifting the consensus target, which could finally bring AAPL stock to the $350 milestone. Apple Says Some AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max Users Must Replace Phones After Service-Loss Bug
Apple (AAPL) said "a small number" of AT&T Inc. (T) customers who recently upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro Max will need to replace their devices after a bug caused them to lose cellular service, multiple outlets reported Friday, citing an Apple statement provided to them.
The bug has prevented some users from making calls, accessing data or sending and receiving texts on the network, leaving devices largely unusable unless connected to Wi-Fi, the reports said.
Apple has issued a carrier settings update and released a new iOS version to prevent the glitch, and affected users will need to swap their phone for a new unit through Apple or AT&T, according to the reports.
"We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls," an Apple spokesperson said, as cited by the reports. It is unclear how many people are affected, the reports said.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment from MT Newswires.

A steady monthlong climb has put a bigger round number on the radar for Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL | AAPL Price Prediction) shareholders. Apple stock is up 10% over the past month to $340 in afternoon trading, and the natural follow-up is what it would take to reach $350. Answering that requires looking past the chart to what Wall Street’s consensus expects, how Apple compares with its peers, and what Apple is actually selling.
For the full-sector context, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), a fund that tracks the NASDAQ 100, is up 5% over the past month to $744.21; thus, in percentage gains, the QQQ ETF trails Apple over that stretch. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stock is up 32% over the past month to $751.41, running far ahead of Apple over the same window. Against that pace, the gain in Apple stock looks modest, even though it exceeded the fund’s advance.
On the other side of the equation, Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock is down 0.7% over the past month to $344.17, which leaves Apple sitting in the middle of its own group. Complicating things further, the analyst consensus target on Apple stock is $328.22, which sits below the current share price. Getting Apple stock to the headline number likely requires analysts to raise that consensus first, since the level in question sits above a price the average target hasn’t yet reached.
Apple Pitches the Mac for Local Artificial Intelligence
Apple is positioning its newest Mac desktops to run demanding artificial intelligence models locally, saving buyers a cloud provider’s fee for each use. According to Apple, the new machines carry substantially more unified memory and bandwidth than the desktops they replace. Those upgrades matter. Large artificial intelligence models lean heavily on fast memory, and more of it lets a single computer handle work that might otherwise go to a data center.
The pitch comes down to cost. For steady workloads, cloud usage bills keep accumulating, and Apple argues capable hardware makes more financial sense over time.
Apple bulls argue that local artificial intelligence gives buyers a concrete reason to pay up for more powerful Macs. That would turn a cost argument aimed at cloud providers into hardware demand Apple can actually book as revenue. Steady Mac orders of that kind would give analysts a tangible reason to revise their targets on Apple stock.
However, the consensus target on Apple stock sits beneath the current share price, so the headline level asks the market to pay more than the average analyst thinks Apple is worth. A single strong product showcase can generate excitement, yet Apple needs sustained buying before the analyst math changes.
What it would take is consistent Mac sales. They need to show up in Apple’s results quarter after quarter, strong enough to push analysts into lifting the consensus above the current share price. Local artificial intelligence gives Apple a credible sales pitch; the next step is proving buyers act on it at scale.
Investors drawn to the local artificial intelligence story should size positions reasonably, since Apple stock already trades above the average analyst target. Balancing exposure against other mega-cap holdings can limit damage if Mac demand proves less durable than hoped.
Shareholders may want to watch for signs that Mac demand tied to local artificial intelligence repeats in Apple’s upcoming quarterly reports. Those reports will reveal if analysts start lifting the consensus target, which could finally bring AAPL stock to the $350 milestone.
